breadcrumb.name: Inverter AC vs Non-Inverter AC: Savings and Payback

sections.h2: Inverter AC vs non-inverter AC savings: where they come from
p: A non-inverter AC has one speed: its compressor runs at full power until the room reaches the setting, switches off, and starts again with a surge. An inverter AC slows its compressor down as the room cools and keeps it running gently, so it draws less on average. With the defaults the difference is 1.8 kW against 1 kW, which over 1,200 hours is 960 units a year.

Both power figures are planning averages, not measurements of your units. The saving is largest in the hottest weeks, when the non-inverter compressor hardly ever switches off, and smallest in mild weather, when it cycles; the second worked example uses the mild-weather figure.

Payback = the extra price ÷ the saving a month. With the example price gap of Rs 40,000 and Rs 35,002 saved a year, that is about 13.7 months of AC use in peak heat, or about 24.9 months if your weather is milder. The price gap is an example to show the method, not a market price; enter the gap between two real quotes for the same brand and tonnage.
Count only the months the AC actually runs. If your payback is two summers, it is two years of calendar time, not two years of AC months.

sections.h2: Is an inverter AC worth it?
p: Usually yes for a room cooled many hours a day at a high slab rate: the saving is largest where hours and tariff are both high. It is less clear for an AC used a few evenings a month or on the protected tariff, where the payback in the table below runs much longer.

Two benefits do not show in the payback: an inverter AC starts without a big surge, so it runs on a smaller generator, UPS or solar inverter, and it keeps the room at a steadier temperature. If you plan to run the AC on solar or a generator, that alone often decides it.

Repair costs differ: an inverter AC's control board is dearer to replace if it fails. Voltage swings shorten the life of both kinds; a stabiliser or a good surge protector protects either. The calculator does not count these because they vary too much to put a fair number on.

faq.q: How much electricity does an inverter AC save?
faq.a: With the planning averages here, about 960 units a year for a 1.5 ton AC run 1,200 hours in peak heat, and about 528 units in milder weather. Your figure depends on hours, weather and the models.

faq.q: What is the payback period of an inverter AC?
faq.a: The extra price ÷ the monthly saving. For the example gap of Rs 40,000, about 13.7 months of AC use in peak heat at Rs 36.46 per unit, longer at lower rates or fewer hours.

faq.q: Is an inverter AC worth it in Pakistan?
faq.a: Usually yes for long daily use at unprotected slab rates, where the payback is short. For a few hours a week or the protected tariff it takes much longer. Its soft start also helps on solar, UPS or a generator.

faq.q: Does an inverter AC save on solar?
faq.a: Yes, twice: it uses fewer units, and it starts without a big surge, so it needs a smaller solar inverter. See how many panels each kind needs with the solar panels for AC calculator.

faq.q: Why does the non-inverter AC use less in mild weather?
faq.a: Its compressor switches off when the room reaches the setting. In mild weather it is off for part of each hour, about 80% on by our planning figure, so its average draw falls and the inverter AC's advantage shrinks.

faq.q: Is the price difference on this page real?
faq.a: No. Rs 40,000 is an example to show the sum, not a market price. Enter the gap between two real quotes for the same brand and tonnage.

key_facts: Yearly saving of an inverter AC = (non-inverter kW − inverter average kW) × hours a year × tariff; payback in months = the extra price ÷ (yearly saving ÷ twelve).
Using a 1.5 ton non-inverter AC at 1.8 kW with its compressor on and an inverter AC at a planning average of 1 kW, 1,200 hours a year save about 960 units, Rs 35,002 at Rs 36.46 per unit.

In milder weather, when the non-inverter compressor runs only about 80% of the hour, the same AC saves about 528 units a year and the payback stretches to about 24.9 months for the same example price gap.
A home on the protected tariff at Rs 13.01 per unit takes about 38.4 months to recover the same example price gap, because each saved unit is worth less.
mistakes: Comparing label watts. The inverter AC's label shows its maximum; the bill follows its average, about 1 kW for a 1.5 ton unit.
Counting calendar months as AC months. Payback is measured in months of AC use; a payback of a summer and a half takes two calendar years.
Comparing different brands or tonnage. The price gap is fair only for the same brand, the same tonnage and the same installation.
Using the peak-summer saving all year. In mild weather the non-inverter AC cycles off and the gap is smaller, as the second example shows.

fields.name: kw_noninv
fields.label: Non-inverter AC power while running
fields.hint: Input watts from the label ÷ 1000. The default is a 1.5 ton non-inverter AC with its compressor on, as in peak summer when it barely switches off. For milder weather, multiply by how much of the hour the compressor runs.

fields.name: kw_inv
fields.label: Inverter AC average power
fields.hint: Average draw over an hour, not the maximum on the label. The default is the planning average for a 1.5 ton inverter AC; a plug-in energy meter gives your own.

fields.name: hours_year
fields.label: Hours the AC runs a year
fields.hint: Hours a day × days of AC weather. The default is 8 hours a day for about five months; Karachi and southern Punjab often run more.

fields.name: tariff
fields.label: Electricity rate
fields.hint: Energy rate of your slab from the bill. The default is the Pakistan unprotected rate for 301 to 400 units a month.

fields.name: price_diff
fields.label: Extra price of the inverter model
fields.hint: Example figure, not a market price. Enter the gap between two real quotes for the same tonnage and brand, installation included.

examples.title: 1.5 ton AC in peak summer, 1,200 hours a year
examples.text: (1.8 − 1) kW × 1,200 h = 960 units × Rs 36.46 = Rs 35,002 a year. The example price gap of Rs 40,000 pays back in about 13.7 months.

examples.title: The same AC in milder weather
examples.text: When the non-inverter compressor runs about 80% of the hour, it averages 1.44 kW. The saving falls to 528 units, Rs 19,251 a year, and payback stretches to about 24.9 months.

examples.title: Long hours: 2,400 hours a year
examples.text: An AC run day and night through a long summer saves 1,920 units, Rs 70,003 a year, and pays back the example gap in about 6.9 months.

examples.title: Protected consumer at Rs 13.01 per unit
examples.text: The same units saved, 960 a year, are worth only Rs 12,490 at the protected rate, so the example gap takes about 38.4 months. Note that an AC usually pushes a home past the protected limit.

content.answer: In peak summer a 1.5 ton inverter AC saves about 960 units a year over a non-inverter AC run 1,200 hours, Rs 35,002 at Rs 36.46 per unit, so an extra price of Rs 40,000 pays back in about 13.7 months. Saving = (non-inverter kW − inverter kW) × hours × tariff; payback = extra price ÷ monthly saving.

formula.text: Payback months = ΔPrice ÷ ((kW_non-inverter − kW_inverter) × hours a year × tariff ÷ 12)
lines: kW_non-inverter = power of the non-inverter AC while it runs (× its on-time share in mild weather)
kW_inverter = average power of the inverter AC over an hour
hours a year = hours a day × days of AC use
tariff = Rs per unit of your slab
ΔPrice = extra price of the inverter model over the non-inverter one

content.safety: Both kinds of AC need their own circuit with the right cable and MCB; an AC on an overloaded socket can overheat the wiring. Have a licensed electrician check the circuit before installing a new AC.
